sections.h2: Who runs a tax sale in Connecticut?
sections.html:
The municipal tax collector does. Connecticut has 169 municipalities, each with its own collector, and the sale procedure in section 12-157 is written for that officer.

When the collector levies a tax warrant on real estate, the collector prepares a notice with the taxpayer's name, a legal description or a citation to the land records, the street address, the amount due as of the last day of the prior month, and the date, time and place of the sale. A statement must say that more taxes, interest and fees accrue after the stated date, so the number on the notice is a floor.

Because each town runs its own sale, scheduling, bidder rules and auction practice vary. The statute lets the collector publish or announce rules for the orderly conduct of the auction, and lets the town hire auctioneers and clerks.

sections.h2: What happens before a house reaches a tax sale?
sections.html:
The usual path begins with an unpaid installment, then interest, then a written demand, and only later a levy. Each step has a statutory trigger.

StageWhat the statute provides
Installment dueTown sets one, two or four payments; last due at least 45 days before fiscal year end (12-142)
DelinquentUnpaid after the first day of the following month; interest at 18 percent per year, $2 minimum (12-146)
DemandCollector makes or sends demand when tax is unpaid 30 days after the due date (12-155)
Levy and noticeWarrant levied on real estate; notices posted; sale scheduled (12-157)
SaleAuction run by the collector; written notice of amounts due posted at the sale (12-157(d))

The sections cited above describe the levy and sale as the collector's procedure, and none of them calls for a lawsuit first. Read the notice you receive for the specific date and place.

sections.h2: How long do I have to redeem after a Connecticut tax sale?
sections.html:
The deadline is not later than six months after the date of the sale. If the property was abandoned, or meets other conditions set by a municipal ordinance, the period can be as short as sixty days. Both rules come from section 12-157(f).

The collector must give notice within sixty days after the sale. The statute calls for publication in a daily newspaper that circulates in the town and for certified mail, return receipt requested, to the delinquent taxpayer and to each mortgagee, lienholder and other encumbrancer of record whose interest is affected. The notice states the sale date, the purchaser's name and address, the price paid and the date the redemption period ends.

The notice also warns what follows if redemption does not happen by that date: titles, mortgages, liens, restraints on alienation and other encumbrances in the property are extinguished. The deed to the purchaser stays with the town clerk, unrecorded, for six months from the sale.

sections.h2: Who else gets notice, and why does that matter to a seller?
sections.html:
Mortgage holders and other lienholders receive the same notice as the owner, because their interests are on the line.

  • The delinquent taxpayer.
  • Each mortgagee of record whose interest is affected.
  • Each lienholder and other encumbrancer with a choate interest.
  • The public, through newspaper publication.

For a seller this means a tax sale is rarely a private problem. A heavy mortgage on a house with tax arrears can pull the lender into the process, and the title company will see the levy in the land records. If you have inherited the house, ask the collector which address the notices went to, so you know what was sent and when.

sections.h2: What can the purchaser do during the redemption period?
sections.html:
The purchaser has limited rights. Under section 12-157(g), during the redemption period the purchaser or the municipality has an insurable interest in the buildings and improvements and may insure them against fire and other risk of physical loss.

The purchaser or the municipality may also petition the superior court for a receiver, or for other equitable relief, if there is imminent danger of damage or destruction to the buildings, or of injury to people or other property from conditions on the lot or on neighboring properties. The statute adds that the purchaser or municipality is not liable, and does not forfeit its interest, solely because it holds the tax deed, for conditions that exist or events that occur during that period.

Ask the collector who bought at the sale and what was paid, since the post-sale notice must state both along with the date redemption ends. Those three facts are what a title company will want to see.

sections.h2: Can I sell before the tax sale or during the redemption period?
sections.html:
Yes, and a sale at either point is how many owners clear the debt. Before a sale, a buyer pays the arrears with interest and charges from the proceeds. After a sale, redemption requires payment of what the statute and collector require, and the closing has to fit inside the redemption window.

The costs on a closing statement are straightforward: the payoff, any mortgage balance, and the conveyance tax if it applies. Under section 12-494, the base rate is three-quarters of one percent to the state and one-quarter of one percent to the municipality on a sale price of $2,000 or more. Tax deeds are among the transfers section 12-498 lists as exempt, but a deed from you to a buyer is a different instrument.

Timing is the main variable. A cash buyer who buys as-is can often move on a short schedule, but a payoff statement, a title search and a signing date still take days. Start well before the sale or redemption deadline, and ask the tax collector for exact figures in writing.

sections.h2: Is there a way to stop a sale altogether?
sections.html:
The sale notice itself warns that taxes, interest and fees keep accruing after the stated amount, so any payoff has to be confirmed with the collector. This page cannot say whether your town takes partial payments or sets up a payment plan, and none of the statutes cited here require it. Ask the office.

You can also contest the underlying tax, within limits. An assessment appeal has a February 20 deadline under section 12-111, and a court application must come within two months of the board's mailed notice under section 12-117a. Neither is a way to stop a sale already scheduled, so use them for the next tax year and call the collector about this one.

Ask these at the tax office, and write down the answers with the date and the name of the person who gave them:

  • How much is owed today, with interest and fees, and the per-day or per-month increase.
  • Whether a warrant has been levied and whether a sale date has been set.
  • Whether a sale has already happened, and if so, the date it will no longer be possible to redeem.
  • The office's written procedure for paying off the account.

faqs.q: Who holds a tax sale in Connecticut?
faqs.a: The municipal tax collector. Each of the state's 169 municipalities runs its own collection and sale, following section 12-157.

faqs.q: How long is the redemption period after a Connecticut tax sale?
faqs.a: Not later than six months after the sale, or sixty days if the property was abandoned or meets conditions set by a municipal ordinance.

faqs.q: What notice must I get after a tax sale?
faqs.a: Within sixty days of the sale, the collector must publish a notice and mail one by certified mail to the taxpayer and to each affected mortgagee and lienholder.

faqs.q: What happens if I do not redeem?
faqs.a: The notice states that titles, mortgages, liens and other encumbrances in the property are extinguished if redemption does not take place by the stated date.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house to stop a tax sale?
faqs.a: Yes. The arrears, interest and charges are paid from the sale proceeds. Ask the tax collector for a written payoff figure and share it with the title company.

faqs.q: Does interest keep running on delinquent Connecticut property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 12-146 sets 18 percent per year, with a $2 minimum per installment unless the town has voted not to impose it.
